analysis.investment_thesis: Riddhi Display fails the Magic Formula on the most important leg — return on capital — with ROE of just 0.61% indicating the business earns essentially nothing on its capital base. A low headline P/E of 4.56 is meaningless when the underlying earnings are so trivial that the "E" is barely positive.
key_strengths: Headline P/E of 4.56 is optically cheap
Debt-light micro-cap with room to scale if execution improves
key_risks: ROE of 0.61% implies near-zero return on capital — fails Magic Formula's quality leg
Tiny INR 23 Cr market cap with negligible institutional interest (FII 0.32%, DII 1.43%) — illiquid
Capital-intensive refrigeration/display manufacturing in a fragmented, low-moat industry
red_flags: ROE <1% — capital is being destroyed in real terms after inflation
Low P/E almost certainly reflects one-off or marginal earnings, not a bargain
Micro-cap with promoter dominance — governance and disclosure risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula requires a company to be both cheap AND good. Riddhi Display passes the first screen superficially (P/E 4.56 implies an earnings yield north of 20%), but completely fails the second: an ROE of 0.61% is among the worst possible signals for a manufacturing business. EBIT/EV cannot be reliably computed without statements, but with profits this thin, even a low EV doesn't rescue the quality score. A business earning sub-1% on equity is functionally a value trap — the cheap multiple exists because the earnings power is fragile and likely non-recurring.

Sectorally, display counters and refrigeration equipment is a capital-intensive, working-capital-heavy, commoditized niche with no pricing power and dominant unorganized competition. With only INR 23 Cr market cap and effectively zero institutional sponsorship, there is neither a quality story nor a catalyst. Greenblatt's systematic approach would rank this very poorly on combined ranking: passable earnings yield, bottom-decile ROC. Skip.
